claims.text: Noodles are wheat-based (the dry tantanmen uses thin Kagawa wheat noodles), and the kitchen runs Sichuan/Chinese dishes with soy-based sauces and fried items, so heavy gluten cross-contact is inherent.
Menu is meat-forward (glazed pork, beef mapo tofu, chicken, pork tantanmen); no vegan dishes or separated plant-based prep were documented.

name: 第一旭 桂店 (Daiichi Asahi Katsura-ten)

claims.text: The broth is described as a pork-bone base seasoned with a deeply flavored soy sauce (shoyu), which in this style is virtually always wheat-containing.
Broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) base and bowls are topped with roast pork, so animal products are integral to the dishes.

name: 大黒ラーメン 本店 (Daikoku Ramen Honten)

claims.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and bowls use a soy-sauce-based tare; no gluten-free handling is offered.
The broth is a tonkotsu-shoyu (pork-bone soy sauce) base; the shoyu tare in this style is virtually always wheat-containing.
Broth is simmered from pork and chicken bones and bowls are topped with char siu pork; there are no vegan items and no separate preparation.

name: だし料理 十 (Dashi Ryori Jifu)

claims.text: The house-made noodles are cut from domestic wheat (and egg) in-house, so flour is handled on-site; a shared-kitchen wheat environment should be assumed.

The signature dashi bowl uses no soy sauce at all — it is seasoned with about 1 gram of Iwate salt only — so the usual wheat-shoyu tare risk is absent from the broth (the wheat comes from the noodles instead).
The dashi is animal-based throughout (sawara/Spanish mackerel and bonito alongside kombu), and the noodles contain egg, so there is no clean vegan or vegetarian path.

Because the owner makes and explains the dashi in front of guests, it is easy to ask exactly what is in the bowl, and the seasoning is unusually transparent: kombu, sawara, bonito, salt, and house wheat-and-egg noodles.
Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in shared water and the menu is built around wheat noodles and a wheat-based soy-sauce tare, so cross-contact with gluten is inherent throughout the kitchen.
Both the ramen tare and the fried rice are soy-sauce based; Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so these dishes contain gluten.
All ramen broths are animal-based (chicken-gara / pork-bone) and bowls include pork back-fat and chashu, so there is no vegan-safe preparation.

name: 元祖熟成細麺 香来 壬生本店 (Ganso Jukusei Hosomen Kourai Mibu Honten)

claims.text: The bowls are built on a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; brewed Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat, and no wheat-free/tamari alternative is indicated.
The shared broth is chicken-bone and pork-bone based and bowls are topped with chashu pork; there is no separate vegan preparation.

name: 吟醸らーめん 久保田 (Ginjo Ramen Kubota)

claims.text: The shoyu ramen and miso tare are made in the standard Japanese ramen style, which relies on wheat-based soy sauce; no wheat-free tare is offered.
All broths and toppings center on pork, chicken and seafood; there is no separate vegetable broth or plant-based preparation line.
